title: Causes and Effects of Migration
subject: AP World History
objectives: Explain the causes of the massive global migrations of the industrial era, including push and pull factors and new transportation technologies (c. 1750–1900)
Describe major migration streams, including European emigration, Asian (Chinese and Indian) labor migration, and systems of indentured and contract labor
Analyze the effects of migration on receiving and sending societies, including new diasporas, ethnic enclaves, demographic change, and nativist backlash
Apply the historical reasoning skill of causation to construct a defensible argument about cause and effect

sections.heading: The Largest Movement of People in History
sections.content:
Between roughly 1840 and 1914, something happened that had never happened before on anything like this scale: tens of millions of human beings left the places their families had lived for centuries and crossed oceans and continents to start new lives. Around 50 to 60 million Europeans left Europe, most for the Americas. Millions of Chinese and Indians fanned out across Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, Africa, and the Pacific. Japanese went to Hawaii and the Americas. By one estimate, more people migrated in this single industrial century than in all of previous recorded history combined. The result is the world's modern human geography — the reason there are huge Italian and Irish communities in the Americas, Indian communities in South Africa and the Caribbean, and Chinese communities across Southeast Asia.

Why did this colossal movement happen exactly now? The answer ties this lesson tightly to the whole unit: it was a CONSEQUENCE OF INDUSTRIALIZATION, in two distinct ways. First, industrialization and imperialism created the FORCES that pushed people to move and pulled them toward new destinations — overpopulation and poverty in some regions, hunger for cheap labor in others. Second, industrial TECHNOLOGY made mass migration physically possible: the steamship turned a perilous months-long ocean crossing into a manageable journey of weeks, and railroads carried migrants deep into continental interiors. Industrialization, in short, both motivated migration and enabled it.

This is also the SYNTHESIS lesson for Unit 6, so beyond the rich content on migration, we will use it to master the historical reasoning skill that anchors this entire unit: CAUSATION. Unit 6 is, at its heart, a unit about cause and effect — industrialization CAUSED imperialism, economic transformation, and these migrations, which in turn had enormous EFFECTS on the whole world. Migration is the perfect topic to learn causation deeply, because it has clear, classifiable causes (push and pull factors) and clear, far-reaching effects. By the end, you will be able to build the kind of causation argument that earns top marks on the AP exam.

sections.heading: Push and Pull: The Causes of Migration
sections.content:
Historians analyze the causes of migration using a simple but powerful framework: PUSH factors (conditions that drive people to leave their home) and PULL factors (conditions that attract them to a destination). Learning to sort causes this way is itself a causation skill, and it maps directly onto the AP exam's love of categorizing causes.

The PUSH factors of the industrial era were often harsh. Rapid POPULATION GROWTH (itself partly a result of better food supply and, later, medicine) left many regions, especially in Europe and Asia, with more people than the land and economy could support. POVERTY and the disruption of traditional rural livelihoods — as industrialization and commercial agriculture displaced peasant farmers and artisans — pushed people off the land. FAMINE was a brutal push: the Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) drove over a million Irish to emigrate and killed roughly a million more. Religious and political PERSECUTION pushed others out, as when Jewish communities fled violent pogroms in the Russian Empire.

The PULL factors drew migrants toward specific destinations. The biggest was ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY — jobs in the booming factories and growing cities of the industrializing world, and above all cheap or free LAND in the Americas and other settler regions (the United States, Canada, Argentina, Australia). The discovery of GOLD (California 1849, Australia 1851, South Africa) pulled hundreds of thousands. And critically for this unit, the global economy of the last lesson created an enormous DEMAND FOR LABOR: plantations growing sugar and rubber, mines digging copper and gold, and great construction projects like railroads and the Panama Canal needed vast numbers of workers — a demand that, as we will see, was met increasingly by Asian labor migration after the abolition of slavery. Notice how every one of these causes traces back to industrialization and the global economy: this is why migration belongs in the 'Consequences of Industrialization' unit.

sections.question: In analyzing the causes of migration, a 'push' factor is...
options: an attraction that draws migrants toward a destination, like jobs or available land
a condition that drives people to leave their home, like famine, poverty, or persecution
the transportation technology that makes migration physically possible
a law that forbids people from leaving their country
sections.explanation: PUSH factors are negative conditions that drive people away from home — famine (the Irish Potato Famine), poverty, overpopulation, displacement of rural livelihoods, and persecution (pogroms). PULL factors are the attractions that draw migrants to a destination (jobs, cheap land, gold). Transportation (steamships, railroads) enabled migration but is not itself a push factor.

sections.heading: Major Migration Streams of the Industrial Era
rows: Population growth, poverty, famine (Irish), persecution; land & jobs
Poverty, instability; demand for labor & gold
Southeast Asia, U.S., Caribbean, Peru, Australia
Poverty; British recruitment after slavery ended
Caribbean, South/East Africa, Fiji, Mauritius, Malaya
Hawaii, U.S. West Coast, Brazil, Peru
Abolition of slavery → labor shortage on plantations

sections.content: Industrial-era technology (steamships, railroads) made possible the largest migration in history, driven by push factors (overpopulation, poverty, famine, persecution) and pull factors (jobs, land, gold, labor demand) — producing European mass emigration and Asian indentured/contract labor migration that created lasting diasporas, reshaped global demographics, and provoked nativist backlash.

sections.heading: Indentured Labor and New Diasporas
sections.content:
One migration stream deserves special attention because it links directly to the abolition of slavery and reshaped societies around the globe: the rise of INDENTURED and CONTRACT LABOR. As the slave trade and then slavery itself were abolished across the 1800s (a reform you met in Unit 5), the plantations and mines of the global economy still hungered for cheap labor. The gap was filled largely by indentured laborers — workers, overwhelmingly from ASIA, who signed (or were pressured into) contracts to work for a set number of years, typically in exchange for passage, low wages, and food. In practice, conditions were often harsh and coercive, leading some historians to call it 'a new system of slavery,' though indentured workers were not legally owned and were, in principle, free at the end of their term.

The two great sources were INDIA and CHINA. The British recruited huge numbers of Indian indentured workers and shipped them across their empire — to sugar plantations in the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Jamaica), to South and East Africa, to Fiji, Mauritius, and Malaya. Chinese laborers (sometimes pejoratively called 'coolies') went to the plantations and mines of Southeast Asia, the guano islands and sugar of Peru, the Caribbean, and the gold fields and railroads of the United States, Canada, and Australia. These migration streams created enduring DIASPORAS — communities of a people living far from their homeland — that permanently changed the ethnic makeup of the receiving societies.

The effects of all this migration ripple through the modern world. Migrants clustered into ETHNIC ENCLAVES (think 'Chinatowns') that preserved language, religion, food, and culture far from home, spreading cultures globally. Migration was also strikingly GENDERED: the majority of migrant laborers were young men, which left many home villages with skewed populations of women, children, and the elderly, and shifted gender roles as women took on new responsibilities. And migration transformed the DEMOGRAPHICS of whole nations — the Americas, Australia, and Southeast Asia became dramatically more diverse. The map of the world's peoples today — where different ethnic and religious communities live — was redrawn in large part by the industrial-era migrations of this lesson.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Building a Causation Argument (the Synthesis Skill)
sections.content:
Because this is the synthesis lesson, let's use migration to build a model CAUSATION argument — the reasoning skill at the heart of Unit 6. Suppose the prompt is: 'Evaluate the extent to which industrialization caused the mass migrations of the period c. 1750–1900.' Watch how a historian turns this into a defensible argument rather than a list of facts.

First, a defensible THESIS that takes a position and previews categories: 'Industrialization was the fundamental cause of the era's mass migrations, both by generating the economic forces — overpopulation, rural displacement, and a vast demand for plantation and industrial labor — that pushed and pulled people across the globe, AND by providing the steamship and railroad technologies that made mass movement physically possible; however, specific triggers such as the Irish famine and the abolition of slavery shaped the particular streams.' Notice this thesis is arguable, it categorizes causes (economic forces vs. enabling technology), and it concedes complexity (specific triggers) — exactly what graders reward.

Second, organize the EVIDENCE by category and distinguish types of cause. ENABLING/underlying causes: industrial steamships and railroads (without which 60 million crossings are impossible) and the integrated global economy's labor demand. PUSH causes: industrial-era population growth and the displacement of peasants and artisans. PULL causes: factory jobs, cheap land, gold. IMMEDIATE triggers: the Irish Potato Famine (a specific spark for Irish emigration) and the abolition of slavery (which created the labor gap that produced Asian indentured migration). Distinguishing long-term/underlying causes from immediate triggers is the single most important move in causation analysis.

Third, EXPLAIN the links and then ASSESS — don't just list. Show the chain: abolition of slavery → labor shortage on plantations → British recruitment of Indian indentured workers → Indian diaspora in the Caribbean and Africa. Then weigh: argue that industrialization was the deepest cause because every other factor (labor demand, the technology, even the population growth) traces back to it, while acknowledging the famine and abolition as crucial proximate triggers. That structure — defensible thesis, categorized and prioritized causes, explained causal chains, and a weighed judgment — is a top-scoring causation response, and it works for any causation prompt on the exam.

sections.question: Which of the following best demonstrates sophisticated CAUSATION analysis rather than simple listing?
options: Naming as many causes of migration as possible without explaining any of them
Distinguishing underlying causes (e.g., the global economy's labor demand) from immediate triggers (e.g., the abolition of slavery), and explaining how they connect to the outcome
Describing what migrant communities looked like once they arrived
Listing the dates of every major migration in order
sections.explanation: Sophisticated causation distinguishes types of cause — underlying/long-term vs. immediate/triggering — and EXPLAINS how they link to the outcome, rather than just listing causes, describing effects, or reciting dates. For example, the abolition of slavery (trigger) created the labor gap that the global economy's demand (underlying cause) filled through Asian indentured migration.

sections.heading: How to Write a Causation Essay (LEQ/DBQ)

steps.title: Write a defensible, categorizing thesis
steps.content: Open with a thesis that takes a clear position on cause/effect AND previews categories of causes (economic, political, technological) or distinguishes cause types. Avoid the vague, generic thesis that Chief Reader reports repeatedly penalize ('There were many causes of migration'). Make it arguable and specific: name WHICH causes mattered most and why.

steps.title: Distinguish underlying causes from immediate triggers
steps.content: Sort your causes into long-term/UNDERLYING (e.g., industrialization, the global labor market) and short-term/IMMEDIATE triggers (e.g., the Irish famine, abolition of slavery). This distinction is the signature move of causation analysis and shows the grader you understand that historical change has layered causes, not one flat list.

steps.title: Use specific evidence and EXPLAIN the causal link
steps.content: Support each cause with specific evidence (the steamship, 50–60 million European emigrants, Indian indentured labor to the Caribbean) and — crucially — EXPLAIN how that cause produced the effect. The phrase 'this led to ___ because ___' is your friend. Explaining the linkage, not just naming the cause, is what earns the evidence and analysis points.

steps.title: Weigh causes and add complexity
steps.content: Argue which cause was most important and defend it, then add COMPLEXITY: acknowledge multiple interacting causes, note effects as well as causes, or compare with another case (e.g., voluntary European emigration vs. coerced indentured labor). A weighed judgment plus nuance earns the complexity point that separates top essays.

sections.heading: Causation Pitfalls and Migration Misconceptions
sections.content: Two sets of traps to avoid. CAUSATION-SKILL pitfalls (flagged in Chief Reader reports): (1) the vague thesis ('there were many causes') — instead categorize and prioritize; (2) LISTING causes without EXPLAINING how each produced the effect; (3) confusing CORRELATION with causation; and (4) failing to distinguish underlying causes from immediate triggers. CONTENT misconceptions about migration: don't treat all migration as voluntary — much industrial-era Asian migration was INDENTURED/CONTRACT labor under harsh, coercive conditions ('a new system of slavery') that arose precisely because slavery was being ABOLISHED. Don't forget the GENDERED pattern (mostly young men migrated, reshaping gender roles in home villages). And don't place these migrations outside their era — the great wave is c. 1840–1914, a CONSEQUENCE of industrialization, not a cause of it.

sections.heading: Remember the Effects — Especially Nativism
sections.content: Causation prompts ask about EFFECTS as well as causes, so have migration's effects ready: new DIASPORAS and ETHNIC ENCLAVES (Chinatowns) that spread cultures globally; dramatic DEMOGRAPHIC change in the Americas, Australia, and Southeast Asia; gendered home societies; and — a high-value, frequently tested effect — NATIVIST BACKLASH. Receiving societies often reacted against immigrants with hostility and discriminatory laws: the U.S. CHINESE EXCLUSION ACT (1882) and the 'White Australia' policy are the textbook examples of governments restricting migration by race/ethnicity. Citing nativism and these specific anti-immigration laws as an EFFECT of migration is exactly the specific, well-chosen evidence that strengthens a causation essay.

sections.heading: Migration Causes & Effects Essentials
sections.content: SCALE: largest migration in history — ~50–60 million Europeans + millions of Chinese, Indians, Japanese, c. 1840–1914. ENABLED BY industrial tech: STEAMSHIPS (weeks not months) + RAILROADS. PUSH factors: overpopulation, poverty, rural displacement, FAMINE (Irish Potato Famine 1845–52), persecution (Russian pogroms). PULL factors: factory JOBS, cheap LAND (U.S., Argentina, Australia), GOLD (California 1849, Australia, South Africa), plantation/mine LABOR DEMAND. INDENTURED/CONTRACT LABOR: rose as SLAVERY was abolished — Indian (British recruited → Caribbean, Africa, Fiji, Mauritius) and Chinese ('coolies' → SE Asia, Peru, U.S. railroads) workers; harsh, semi-coercive. EFFECTS: lasting DIASPORAS & ETHNIC ENCLAVES (Chinatowns); global culture spread; DEMOGRAPHIC change; GENDERED migration (mostly young men); and NATIVIST BACKLASH → CHINESE EXCLUSION ACT (1882, U.S.), 'White Australia' policy. SYNTHESIS SKILL — CAUSATION: defensible categorizing thesis; distinguish UNDERLYING causes from IMMEDIATE triggers; EXPLAIN (not list) causal links; weigh causes + add complexity.

sections.heading: Closing Unit 6: A World Remade by Industrial Power
sections.content:
Step back and see Unit 6 whole, because it completes the great hinge of the modern world that began in Unit 5. Unit 5 built the engine — the Enlightenment's ideas, the political revolutions, and above all industrialization. Unit 6 shows that engine's CONSEQUENCES rolling across the entire planet, and the unifying thread is exactly the skill you just practiced: CAUSATION. Industrialization was the great cause; everything in this unit is its effect. It CAUSED the new imperialism, as a few industrial powers used their overwhelming military and technological edge to seize most of Africa and Asia (Lesson 1). It provoked a whole spectrum of indigenous RESPONSES — resistance, rebellion, and reform — that, though mostly crushed in the short run, seeded the nationalism that would later end empire (Lesson 2). It built a single, integrated, but deeply UNEQUAL global economy, organized so that an industrial core extracted wealth from a dependent periphery through both colonies and economic imperialism (Lesson 3). And it set in motion the largest human MIGRATION in history, redrawing the map of the world's peoples (this lesson). Pull the camera back and the unit is one causal story: industrial power remaking the world.

Now hold change and continuity together, the way the exam rewards. The CHANGES of c. 1750–1900 were staggering: a handful of nations came to dominate the globe; the world economy was integrated into a single market; and tens of millions of people relocated across oceans. But notice the CONTINUITIES that complicate any simple narrative of progress. Long-distance trade networks, the spread of cultures and religions, large-scale migrations, and the exploitation of distant labor are not new — you saw them in the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean of Unit 2 and the maritime empires and Atlantic slave trade of Unit 4. What changed was the SCALE, the SPEED (industrial technology), and the DEGREE of inequality and domination. The pattern continued; its intensity exploded. That 'continuity in form, transformation in scale' is precisely the kind of nuanced CCOT/causation insight that earns complexity points.

Most importantly, see what this unit hands forward. The empires, the racial ideologies, the global inequalities, the rival industrial nation-states bristling with new weapons, the nationalism rising in both the imperial powers and their colonies — all of it is loaded and ready. In the very next unit you will watch these pressures detonate into the most destructive conflicts in human history: the World Wars (Unit 7). The colonized peoples' resistance will mature into the decolonization movements of Unit 8. And the integrated, unequal global economy will evolve into the globalization debates of Unit 9. Unit 6 is where the modern world's power structures, and its deepest injustices, were set. Master its causal logic — industrialization as the engine, imperialism, economic transformation, and migration as its world-shaking effects — and you hold the key to everything that follows.

Connect forward to the World Wars (Unit 7), decolonization (Unit 8), and globalization (Unit 9). On the exam this is core for MCQ on migration causes/effects and indentured labor, and for CAUSATION LEQ/DBQ/SAQ prompts across the modern era.
